text: This lab pulls the last three lessons into one real decision. A platform upgrade is scheduled four months out. Three teams share this instance: Facilities ships weekly on a small booking app, Fulfillment ships quarterly on a heavily-used order management app with a deprecated API dependency, and Partner Integrations ships unpredictably whenever an external partner's API changes. You're the architect getting this instance through the upgrade cleanly.

Step one is identifying the highest-risk customization, using the criteria from Lesson 23 and Lesson 21 together. Usage volume: the order management app is touched constantly. Deprecated-dependency risk: it relies on an API already flagged for removal next release, exactly the aging-dependency pattern that gets riskier every cycle it survives. Blast radius: if it breaks, fulfillment operations stop directly. That combination makes it the clear highest-risk item, well above the booking app or the partner connector.

Step two prioritizes pre-upgrade sandbox testing. The order management app goes into the high-risk tier and gets tested first, with existing automated test coverage plus manual regression focused specifically on the code paths touching the deprecated API. Testing it first, rather than last, leaves maximum runway to fix any real blocker before the upgrade date. The booking app gets a lighter spot-check later, and the partner connector gets evaluated case by case depending on how recently its API actually changed.

Step three negotiates the release freeze window, following Lesson 22's governance approach rather than imposing one team's convenience on everyone. A two-week freeze goes on the shared calendar at month four, not two weeks before it starts. Facilities' weekly cadence pauses briefly, at low cost. Fulfillment's quarterly release gets scheduled to land before the freeze entirely, so it doesn't compete with upgrade validation for the same testing bandwidth. Partner Integrations gets an expedited critical-fix path for anything genuinely urgent, since the organization doesn't control when the partner's API changes.

Step four communicates on the real timeline from Lesson 21. At month four, every stakeholder gets the upgrade date, the freeze dates, and the reasoning behind the testing priority. At month one, the sandbox is upgraded and Fulfillment's testing begins. In the final two weeks, the freeze is active, the lighter checks wrap up, and a documented go or no-go decision gets made with Fulfillment's results as the primary evidence.

No team gets silently steamrolled, the highest-risk application gets the attention its dependency and usage actually warrant, and the freeze is negotiated months ahead rather than discovered the week it starts. That's lessons 21 through 23 working as one coherent decision. Next up, Chapter 8 opens with platform governance models.
